shortlist.raw_text: System One models promise fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. However, understanding their capability spectrum and decision reliability requires more than aggregate performance on current benchmarks. Existing evaluations often provide limited insight into the breadth of model capabilities and the reliability of their decisions. We introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark characterizing the capability spectrum and decision reliability of System One models across 11 domains and five capability families. For the capability spectrum, SO-Arena offers evidence-grounded evaluation through reliable sources and manual verification of reference labels against model-visible inputs; fine-grained capability assessment through domain-specific difficulty criteria; and realistic interactive evaluation, where models iteratively execute actions in sandboxes. Reasoning-intensive tasks further enable system one-two comparison. Beyond accuracy, SO-Arena assesses decision reliability through two complementary measures: decision stability under controlled option-set changes and missing-answer recognition when no valid option is available. Evaluations across 21 models reveal that the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. More importantly, strong overall performance does not necessarily imply reliable decision-making: the best-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. Together, these findings highlight the need to characterize capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary dimensions, providing a systematic view of the strengths and limitations of System One models.

shortlist.raw_text: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman . That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely . But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere . This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair . Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube , where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder . Thanks so much. Great to be here. This requires plausible motion of surrounding vehicles as well as precise ego-trajectory control. shortlist.raw_text: Driving world models aim to simulate how a scene unfolds under different ego actions. This requires plausible motion of surrounding vehicles as well as precise ego-trajectory control. Learning vehicle motion from perspective video alone is challenging because motion is entangled with appearance and vehicles can be occluded. Prior work therefore conditions video generation on layouts that specify vehicle motion, providing control over surrounding vehicles but requiring their future trajectories as inputs. We introduce BirdDreams, an autoregressive driving world model that jointly generates perspective video and a schematic bird's-eye-view (BEV) video, making scene layout part of the predicted future. The BEV, rendered from scene annotations for training, depicts roads and vehicles as simple shapes at a fixed metric scale, providing a top-down view of their positions and motion with reduced occlusion between vehicles. Perspective video, by contrast, retains scene details that the BEV omits, such as traffic signals and object appearance. Joint attention between two video diffusion transformers, one per stream, lets each stream inform the other during generation. The predicted BEV also provides a geometric interface for ego control: we translate and rotate its latest frame along an input ego trajectory and use the resulting frames as a soft condition that shows how the scene would appear to move if only the ego vehicle moved. At inference, BirdDreams generates both videos from a single camera image without requiring an HD map or vehicle-state inputs. On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, BirdDreams follows input ego trajectories more faithfully than prior driving world models and generates more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning. Human evaluation shows that BirdDreams outperforms a perspective-only baseline in generating realistic surrounding-vehicle behavior.

shortlist.raw_text: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos. We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.

Title: Anthropic CEO Amodei admits "there's a huge uncertainty in what's going to happen next year" days before a record IPO

Text:
Days before what could be the largest IPO in history, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called buying compute 'the deepest business dilemma' his company faces. Anthropic's commitments now total nearly $901 billion, and it's still far from clear whether future revenue will justify those costs. The planned IPO is largely meant to serve as a financial buffer against that uncertainty. The article Anthropic CEO Amodei admits "there's a huge uncertainty in what's going to happen next year" days before a record IPO appeared first on The Decoder .

Article text (excerpt):
Days before what could be the largest IPO in history, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei names the central weakness of his business model. Nobody knows how the company's compute investments will pay off, he says. It isn't the first time he's sounded this warning.
"There's a huge uncertainty in what's going to happen next year." Speaking at a JPMorgan Chase investor event in New York on Friday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei used that line to sum up the problem facing his company.
The admission came, of all times, in the last days before the company's planned Nov. 19 IPO, and compute was one of several topics in the conversation. Speaking with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon , he said, "Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces." Ad
AI technology is advancing so fast that, Amodei said, no one yet knows how that progress will translate into economic value. But compute has to be bought one to two years ahead, before anyone knows whether revenue will justify the cost. Ad
If Anthropic buys too little, he said, it won't have the resources for customers and new technologies, and revenue takes a hit. Buying too much carries the opposite risk. "You can financially overextend yourself," Amodei said.
Anthropic has already committed nearly $901 billion, most of it to compute and chips, according to Bloomberg . Roughly $71 billion of that comes due by September 2027. Bloomberg notes that figure exceeds the market cap of about two-thirds of S&P 500 companies. Ad
Back in February 2026, Amodei warned in much sharper terms that he could buy $1 trillion of compute starting at the end of 2027 and go bankrupt if revenue fell short. Being off by just one year could mean bankruptcy. He is not sure some competitors have done the math, and he said they don't really understand the risks they're taking. The stakes have kept rising since then.
Amodei described two ways Anthropic softens the compute dilemma: gross margins and cash on the balance sheet. He said the company’s gross margins are "quite good," especially compared with other players, and that Anthropic has a large cash balance and is seeking to raise more. Ad
The company also buys relatively little compute upfront, then can turn to the spot market for additional capacity if business goes better than expected. Amodei compared that approach to buying insurance, saying it leaves Anthropic covered if results fall short while allowing it to invest more when things go well. Ad
The compute bets were the biggest reason to go public: the more cash Anthropic holds, he said, the wider its margin for error between a world with too little compute and one with too much.
Anthropic plans to raise up to $64.4 billion through the IPO and another $26 billion through a private placement, Bloomberg reports. Combined, that would make it the largest IPO ever. The offering is reportedly already about six times oversubscribed .
Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate hit $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from late September, according to company filings. Bloomberg says the rising popularity of AI products, including its coding models, has helped fuel revenue growth.
Amodei struck a relaxed tone about the IPO's timing, saying he wasn't fixated on a specific month or particular market conditions. Anthropic, he noted, grew from nothing to its current size in just six years. The most common advice he got before the IPO, or the advice that resonated most, he said, was something like "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's really worth." That, he said, is very similar to a model Anthropic uses internally: "under-promise and over-deliver."
In the same conversation, though, Amodei said he hopes AI will cure cancer and Alzheimer's within five to 15 years, adding that he doesn't know exactly. In Silicon Valley, that may already count as under-promising.

text:
Anthropic is heading into the largest IPO in history with a startling warning.

Its CEO called buying AI compute the single deepest business dilemma his company faces.

The numbers explain why.

AI technology advances fast, but compute must be ordered one to two years ahead. 

If Anthropic buys too little, it loses customers to competitors. If it buys too much, it risks financial overextension.

The scale of that hardware bet is staggering:
• $901 billion total committed to compute and chips
• $71 billion coming due by September 2027
• $64.4 billion targeted in the IPO, plus $26 billion in private placement

That $71 billion obligation alone exceeds the market cap of about two-thirds of S&P 500 companies.

Anthropic reached an $81 billion annualized revenue run rate at the end of October. Yet Amodei noted that being off on hardware timing by even a single year could mean bankruptcy. 

The company softens the risk by keeping cash on hand, using spot markets for extra capacity, and keeping gross margins strong. The record IPO is less a celebration and more a giant cushion against an unpredictable market.

My read: the hardest part of building frontier AI right now isn't writing code. It's having a balance sheet large enough to survive guessing wrong on hardware capacity two years out.

How does your team handle capital commitments when the payback window is completely unproven?

Source: The Decoder
